question:
A 47-year-old male presents with a one-week history of diminished hearing in his right ear and a
sensation of ear “popping” when yawning or swallowing. He denies ear pain or drainage but reports a

recent episode of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and mild cough that resolved a week ago. His medical
history includes hypertension and mild intermittent epistaxis, and his medications include lisinopril and
daily baby aspirin. He does not smoke or consume alcohol. On examination, he is afebrile. The right
tympanic membrane appears dull, mildly retracted, and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy, with similar
but less severe findings in the left ear. Anterior rhinoscopy shows normal turbinates and nasal mucosa,
without blood, polyps, or lesions. The throat and neck exams are unremarkable. Which of the following
is the most appropriate approach for managing this patient’s ear condition? Answer Choices: (A)
Fluticasone nasal spray once daily until symptoms resolve (B) Pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 4 to 6
hours until symptoms resolve (C) Saline nasal irrigation twice daily for 2 weeks (D) Referral to an
otolaryngologist for further evaluation (E) Observation alone (F) Oral pseudoephedrine for symptomatic
relief (G) Oral prednisone taper to reduce inflammation (H) Application of topical ciprofloxacin drops to
the affected ear (I) Antihistamine therapy to reduce eustachian tube dysfunction (J) Myringotomy with
tympanostomy tube placement
 A. Oral pseudoephedrine for symptomatic relief
B. Application of topical ciprofloxacin drops to the affected ear
C. Referral to an otolaryngologist for further evaluation
D. Pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 4 to 6 hours until symptoms resolve
E. Antihistamine therapy to reduce eustachian tube dysfunction
F. Myringotomy with tympanostomy tube placement
G. Oral prednisone taper to reduce inflammation
H. Saline nasal irrigation twice daily for 2 weeks
I. Fluticasone nasal spray once daily until symptoms resolve
J. Observation alone
